finding.claim: The caller's identity is taken straight from the client-supplied request header X-Session-User-Verified, with no session, signature or token check. Any client can send the header with the name of a user who holds grants on a file and then delete or rename that file. The 'Verified' in the header name suggests a trusted proxy sets it, but nothing in this code strips or authenticates it. The attack works unless an upstream proxy overwrites or removes the header on every request.
finding.source: HTTP request header X-Session-User-Verified, sent by an unauthenticated remote client
finding.sink: ensure_allowed/is_allowed authorization decision (acl.py:5) guarding del STORE[fid] (views.py:18) and f['name'] assignment (views.py:27)

trace.note: is_allowed looks up the spoofed user name in resource['grants']
POST /files/<fid>/rename runs the same check for 'write'

finding.guards_checked: Searched the whole codebase (two files) for any authentication, middleware or signature verification of the header and found none. A missing header gives g.user=None, which is denied, so only a spoofed valid user name gets through. I could not see any proxy or gateway configuration that would strip the header.

verdict.guard_found: ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10, aborts 403) and is_allowed (acl.py:4-5, result tested at views.py:25) work correctly, but they only check the header-supplied name against grants. Nothing authenticates the header. No proxy or middleware config exists in the repo (only acl.py and views.py).
verdict.reason: views.py:11 sets g.user directly from the client-controlled X-Session-User-Verified header, and the ACL checks at views.py:17 and views.py:25 (acl.py:5) only compare that name to grants, so an unauthenticated client who sends a granted user's name can reach views.py:18 and views.py:27. This is only exploitable if no upstream proxy strips or overwrites the header, which can't be seen from the code.
